where: Section 2 and the figure data (actual series) versus the threshold definition in Section 1
problem: The chapter defines the threshold as the input CNR where the output SNR is 1 dB below the above-threshold law. But the plotted 'actual' curve puts the output at 20 dB for 10 dB input, against an ideal 25.7 dB — a 5.7 dB shortfall, not 1 dB. So in the chapter's own numbers the knee is not at 10 dB; the curve has already broken away several dB above it. A student who applies the definition to the figure will get a threshold of roughly 11–12 dB, and the sentence 'Below roughly 10 dB they break away' contradicts the data point at 10 dB.
fix: Make the figure and the text agree. Either (a) keep the 1 dB definition and move the curve so the actual point at 10 dB is about 24.7 dB, with the steep drop starting near 10 dB and 1 dB deviation reached at 10 dB; or (b) keep the steeper curve and state that the threshold here is about 11–12 dB input CNR, changing 'At 10 dB input the actual output is about 20 dB' to 'At 10 dB input the output is already about 20 dB, roughly 6 dB below the ideal line, so this receiver's 1 dB threshold lies near 11–12 dB.'

problem: 'the stronger one suppresses the weaker by a few dB' is vague: it mixes the size of the suppression with the capture ratio and can be read as saying the weaker signal is merely reduced a few dB, when in fact it is largely rejected once the capture ratio is exceeded.
fix: Write: 'of two co-channel FM signals, the stronger one takes over the detector output and the weaker is effectively rejected, provided the stronger exceeds it by the capture ratio, typically a few dB.'
